Manchester United have triggered their one-year option on captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.
The 32-year-old's deal was due to expire next summer but sources say both parties decided it was in their best interests to activate the option through to 2028.
It means overseas clubs will not be able to approach Fernandes when the transfer window opens on 1 January.
The Portugal international confirmed on Tuesday that discussions over a new contract had been paused. Sources say they will resume once United's league position has improved.
Fernandes has made 343 appearances for United, scoring 115 goals, since his £47m move from Sporting in January 2020.
Last season he broke the Premier League assists record and scooped all of the individual player of the year awards after an outstanding campaign as United finished third.
While there is doubt over his long-term future, extending the contract means United would be able to command a fee for Fernandes should he leave in the summer.
United had been open to selling Fernandes in the summer of 2025, with Saudi Pro-League club Al Hilal offering a huge deal.
After discussing the situation with his wife, Fernandes decided to stay, though he later said it "hurt" United were willing to sell him. He reiterated on Tuesday he was still ambitious to win the biggest honours in the game.
Fernandes is a doubt for Saturday's Premier League encounter with Brentford after returning from the Champions League trip to Sporting with a virus.
The playmaker, who scored both goals in the 2-2 draw with his former club, but did not train on Friday and head coach Mauricio Pochettino said he would take a decision on his captain's fitness on Saturday morning.
"We are going to assess during the day and then tomorrow see how he is when he wakes up," said Pochettino. "We are not going to take any risks."
Pochettino is preparing for his first home game as Man Utd boss
Pochettino was criticised by former Liverpool and England midfielder Jamie Redknapp on the Overlap earlier this week.
Reference was made to the former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea coach high-fiving Sky Sports reporter Patrick Davidson after his side's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday, as evidence Pochettino had lost his edge.
"When I saw Pochettino at Southampton and I saw him at Tottenham, he looked like he had that Argentinian dog in him," said Redknapp.
"I look at him now and he's high-fiving everyone, he's got the bracelets on, he's got the barnet. I think he's gone too nice."
It seems someone had mentioned the observation to Pochettino as he went off on a tangent at his Friday news conference when asked about a "crazy" first week that included red cards, refereeing errors, disallowed goals and a drone filming training.
"What are we going to do? Start to cry?" he asked. "No. We have to be strong, believe and keep going. I cannot judge the past. Who am I to do that? I was in Cincinnati. I was outside. I need to shut my mouth, say nothing and start from now.
"Sometimes we are so confusing two words that means something similar; nice and good. I am not nice. We have to be good. It is a different thing. We know when we need to push, when we need to be strong, and when we need to build something to improve the atmosphere and relationship and everything.
Pochettino also confirmed £70m midfielder Carlos Baleba is expected to be out until the last week in January with the hamstring injury he sustained against Roma on 3 November.
Forward Marcus Rashford had begun to do individual work outside as he tries to recover from a hip problem that has kept him out since 13 October.

Manchester City have managed only five clean sheets this season
Manchester City 's leaky defence faces one of its most difficult tasks of the season with a trip to watertight Arsenal , aiming to put right their patchy recent form.
Enzo Maresca's side began the season with eight straight victories but have won only one of their past seven in all competitions inside 90 minutes and head to Emirates Stadium trailing the champions by six points even at this early juncture.
A Premier League defeat on Sunday could well have long-term consequences for City's title aspirations, with Mikel Arteta's men clearly standing above any other top-flight side as the ones to topple.
Though the Gunners dropped points last weekend with a draw at Newcastle , they continue to set the standards with a miserly defence that has conceded only seven goals in the club's opening 11 league games.
Asked why he felt City have dropped off in recent weeks, Maresca - who replaced Pep Guardiola as manager in the summer - said: "For me it's because we've had four months together. Transition requires time.
"It's probably because we won seven games in a row, with Champions League eight in a row. Everyone was thinking at City there's no transition but I've said many times I am not a magician. There is transition, it's normal.
"There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new so you need time and you can see different clubs when they had transition how complicated it is. For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all."
'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt
"We are conceding too many goals and we need to avoid that," was an obvious statement made by Maresca following last Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham.
City followed that up with another home stalemate against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday and have now conceded in 10 successive games in all competitions for the first time in seven years.
"[It was] far, far too easy to play through [City]," said former England captain Alan Shearer of Rodrigo Muniz's goal for Fulham on Match of the Day.
" Fulham 's throw-in was level with their own 18-yard box. For them to get through is not acceptable at any level, let alone when you are playing for Manchester City and Muniz ran past the entire midfield [to score]."
City have managed only five clean sheets all campaign, which is in stark contrast to Arsenal , who have kept double the amount so far, while Newcastle 's opening goal ended a run off 445 minutes without the ball hitting their net.
Maresca's men also have an issue by conceding the opener, having done so seven times in the past 10 games, and of the 14 goals they have shipped, six have come inside the first 20 minutes.
An early Arsenal goal may well be an important factor in deciding Sunday's contest.
Asked how his side can improve defensively, Maresca said: "Video [analysis], meetings, [on] pitch coaching, It is a mix of that.
"Some of the goals we concede we can avoid, so hopefully we can do that."
Man City fan questions what's behind Marc Guehi's recent struggles
The injury to key defender William Saliba has almost gone unnoticed for Arsenal as Ezri Konsa has stepped in to fill the void at centre-back seamlessly since joining from Aston Villa in the summer.
The England international has established a formidable partnership with Gabriel and the two have quickly formed an impressive understanding this season.
Maresca, meanwhile, admitted he was still "trying to find different" solutions to his team, which has been highlighted by the chopping and changing of his backline.
In 16 Premier League and Champions League games this season, the Italian has used eight different combinations in defence, which has given players little chance of fostering any sort of on-pitch relationships with each other.
City have also made seven errors leading to goals, compared to Arsenal 's one.
"You are concerned in some way because that is a lot of errors leading to goals," said former City defender Nedum Onuoha. "With some of the best players you ask, 'what are they really good at?' For some it is the fact they don't make mistakes.
"They are ruthless and relentless in the way they play but at this moment in time City are being punished for those errors.
"A manager can have the tactics and do the team talks, but if people are going to continue to make those mistakes, they will suffer."
The chant of "1-0 to the Arsenal " has been synonymous with the Gunners over the years and it could not be more apt under Arteta.
Since the start of last season, his side have won 16 matches in all competitions by that particular scoreline, compared to six by City.
After beating Sunderland in a chaotic match in September, Maresca said he would "prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3", suggesting his side needed more control and he re-iterated that message after the Fulham draw.
"Sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference and to keep a clean sheet but in this moment we are not able to do that," he admitted.
City, though, have scored five more league goals than Arsenal in this campaign and Sunday's hosts have injury concerns over goalkeeper David Raya.
The Spaniard is a doubt with the shoulder problem he picked up at Newcastle , and compatriot Kepa Arrizabalaga may deputise again as he did in the 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday.
City have fond memories of coming up against Arsenal 's stand-in keeper, after Kepa's howler for the opening goal contributed to their 2-0 Carabao Cup final triumph back in March.
A repeat result on Sunday will provide a much-needed morale boost for Maresca and his team.

Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights
Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning , the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.
Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.
While the judgment was celebrated by some in Quebec who considered it a vindication of the province’s fight, it was swiftly criticised by religious civil liberties groups.
“We cannot exist in a country as free people, where governments can literally go to the electorate and say, ‘I’m gonna take away the rights of a certain group of minorities’, because it’s popular and to play wedge politics with the charter rights of Canadians,” Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters at a press conference. “If that is the case, we don’t have a charter of rights and freedoms. We have a charter of suggestions and permissions.”
Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.
Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The clause is the result of political compromise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.
Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters .
In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.
Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in an attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96 , which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.
But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional rights and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.
In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.
In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.
In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.
The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.
The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws was at risk.
Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.
The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."
The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.
On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.
The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
Canada's top court to rule on Quebec's ban on wearing religious symbols
Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.
Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.
"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-François Blanchet told reporters in French.

Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances
Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.
The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.
The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.
The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February.
Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers .
In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.
“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”
He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”.
However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted.
In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks.
It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.”
The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet.
Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air , whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic.
Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners.
However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

Manchester United have triggered their 12-month option to extend captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.
His deal was previously set to expire at the end of this season but will now run until summer 2028.
United have been in talks with Fernandes over extending his contract since the summer.
Sky Sports News understands both parties are in agreement that it makes sense to return to negotiations in the future - with full focus on improving the club's current position.

Fernandes is understood to be under the weather and is being kept away from the squad ahead of the Brentford game.
On whether he'll make the game, Mauricio Pochettino said: "We don't know. He got a virus in Portugal. He finished the game with a problem and today he cannot be part of the training session.

"What triggering this option does is reduce the chance to zero that any club outside of the Premier League can approach Fernandes from Europe's top leagues around a potential move next summer for free.
"So this move protects both the club and the player from that situation.
"We know he's been the subject of interest in the last few summers, especially from Saudi Arabia.

Fernandes has rejected two contract offers from United . The club's initial proposal was made in the summer when discussions first began over a new deal, but was turned down by the Portuguese, who signed his last contract in August 2024.
The United captain said: "I've seen people saying that he's asked for more money, he's asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn't be here.
"I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.
"Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here. The thing is, I've always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it's time for me to move on, I will move on.
"I'm not going to be the player that I've seen many in this time at Manchester United. They're going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, 'Bruno, it's time to part ways', I'm going to be the first one walking out the door.

"My aim will always be to win the Premier League and the Champions League within the club I am."
Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada also spoke to Sky Sports last week about Fernandes' contract talks and said: "Listen, I've said before, we have a tremendous amount of respect for Bruno. We're very fortunate to have him as a captain.

"And we're very proud to have him as captain. It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private. I think it's something that needs to be discussed behind the scenes between him and the club."

Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.
Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".
The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

The planned withdrawal will end Uganda's nearly two-year campaign against ADF militants in Lubero
Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from a town in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours.
The troops will hand over security in Lubero, in North Kivu province, to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations, the Ugandan army said in a statement on Friday.
The announcement comes days after DR Congo summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over controversial social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni.
The Ugandan military did not give a reason for the withdrawal or say whether it was linked to the diplomatic row.
The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) Islamist group fleeing joint military operations elsewhere in eastern DR Congo.
The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, is affiliated to the Islamic State and has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries.
Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign in November 2021, following a series of bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said that the joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, would continue elsewhere in DR Congo.
Five years into the joint offensive, the ADF remains DR Congo's deadliest armed group, despite a significant decline in its activities in Uganda, according to the conflict monitoring organisation Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled).
John Ngono, Acled's DR Congo analyst, said the group was killing an average of four civilians a day and had expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo.
He said the findings suggested that "Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC".
Acled says the group has not carried out an attack in Uganda since June 2025, but its growing interest in mineral resources in DR Congo could help finance its operations and sustain its ability to threaten both countries.
The planned withdrawal comes amid strained relations between Uganda and DR Congo, despite years of close military co-operation.
Earlier this week, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to endorse a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo, threatening that Ugandan troops would seize it themselves if the rebels failed to do so.
The Congolese foreign ministry described his remarks as "particularly serious" and demanded that Uganda clarify its official position and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Gen Kainerugaba also defended Uganda's military presence in eastern DR Congo, insisting it was driven by security concerns.
The planned withdrawal comes amid renewed fighting between Congolese forces and rebels in the wider Lubero territory, raising fresh concerns about the safety of civilians.
Eastern DR Congo has endured decades of conflict involving dozens of armed groups, with millions of people forced to flee their homes.

Passengers advised to seek refunds via bankruptcy process, though guarantees are not assured, warns Norse Atlantic.
Norwegian budget airline Norse Atlantic said it would file for bankruptcy for its main Norwegian operating unit and has stopped selling tickets, becoming the latest airline casualty of fuel-cost spikes stemming from the war in Iran..
The airline has cancelled all flights and said on its website that its customer service department is no longer available.
The shutdown came quickly. On Wednesday, the airline, which was founded in 2021, said its financial situation was “critical”. A day later, it suspended flights and warned that it could file for bankruptcy if it failed to secure funding.
By Friday, the airline said it could not raise the money it needed to continue flying.
Norse is the latest airline to struggle with rising fuel costs brought on by the US-led war in Iran. Latvia’s airBaltic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September, while US budget airline Spirit Airlines went out of business in May.
Jet fuel prices have risen 71 percent globally over the past year and more than 78 percent in Europe, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA) which tracks jet fuel prices.
“We were unable to absorb the extra cost … Fuel is what toppled this company,” CEO Eivind Roald told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
Norse said on its website that passengers could seek refunds through the bankruptcy process but warned that refunds were not guaranteed. It advised customers to check their travel insurance or contact their banks.
“This is a very hard day for the pilots and their families, and for all other Norse employees. Our thoughts are also with the passengers whose journeys are now cancelled,” the board of the Norse Atlantic Pilots Association told the Reuters news agency.
The airline also began ending its aircraft leasing agreements with AerCap Holdings and BOC Aviation, which were for 12 and 16 years, respectively.
Norse’s shares fell nearly 69 percent on the Oslo Stock Exchange on Friday, bringing its losses this year to 99.86 percent. In the US, its shares fell 85 percent on Friday, trading at a fraction of a cent.

Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.
"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".
Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.
He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.
Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.
An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.
Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October
Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."
The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.
For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.
Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.
Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November
Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.
But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.
Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."
But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.
Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with
British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.
The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.
The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz , a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.
Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.
More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.
A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks…

Uganda's army on Friday said it planned to withdraw from the eastern DR Congo town of Lubero in North Kivu. The announcement came days after Ugandan army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba – son of President Yoweri Museveni – threatened to take control of Walikale, another North Kivu town, sparking a diplomatic spat between the two neighbouring nations.
Uganda 's army said on Friday it planned to withdraw from a key DR Congo town and accused militias apparently allied to the Congolese government of stepping up attacks in the strife-torn eastern region.
The Ugandan announcement comes days after the DRC said it had summoned the Ugandan embassy's head of mission over remarks by the country's army chief.
The mineral-rich eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has been wracked by violence for more than 30 years, often drawing in its neighbours Uganda and Rwanda directly or through support for local armed groups.
Read more UN Security Council demands Rwanda withdraw troops from eastern DR Congo
Ugandan armed forces (UPDF) have been deployed in Ituri and North Kivu provinceson the DRC's border with Uganda since 2021.
They were sent to back up the Congolese army against militants linked to the Islamic State jihadist group.
The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), historically a Ugandan rebel coalition, was established in the eastern DRC in 1995 and regularly carries out killings in the deeply troubled region plagued by myriad armed groups.
The Congolese army is also fighting the armed FRN anti-governmental group, formerly known as the M23 , which is backed by Rwanda, in the region.
Watch more Predictable: DR Congo-Rwanda rivalry spills over to Francophonie summit
On Monday, Ugandan army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of President Yoweri Museveni , threatened on X to take control of the strategic Congolese town of Walikale in North Kivu province.
The FRN launched an offensive towards the town at the beginning of the month.
Kainerugaba – known for inflammatory posts on social media – had in a separate post also called for the unconditional surrender of the airport in Isiro, the provincial capital in Haut-Uele.
In response, Kinshasa announced the following day the summons of the Ugandan diplomat following what it called the "particularly serious" remarks.
The DRC "remains determined to ensure respect for its dignity and its institutions in the face of any form of provocation or interference", it said in a statement.
On Friday, the Ugandan army spokesman said on X that it would "soon" withdraw its forces from the town of Lubero in North Kivu which is close to a front line in fighting between Congolese and FRN forces.
Watch more Uganda withdraws troops from peacekeeping mission in Somalia
In a separate post, the spokesman accused militia forces, including some apparently allied to the Congolese government, of stepping up attacks on civilians.
"These negative militia forces have increasingly mounted attacks against vulnerable communities, massacring women and children such as the Bahema and Tutsi communities in Ituri and the North Kivu region," he said.
"Under International Humanitarian Law (IHL), the UPDF retains the responsibility to extend protection to such vulnerable communities and will continue to do so whenever possible," he added.

A Levski Sofia supporter has been filmed appearing to perform a Nazi salute in the stands during Marseille’s Europa League tie against the Bulgarian side, in footage that has circulated widely online. The clip emerged amid chaotic scenes at the Stade Vélodrome , where flares and other projectiles were thrown and rival supporters clashed before and during Thursday’s match.
Around 500 Levski fans were housed in the away section. About ten minutes before kick-off , several Marseille supporters ran from a home stand and breached the away enclosure, apparently targeting the Bulgarian fans. Projectiles and flares were thrown between the two groups, and further disturbances broke out during the half-time break.
Five Levski Sofia supporters were taken to hospital with injuries including eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder, according to the Marseille police prefecture . Around a dozen Bulgarian fans were reportedly injured in total. Despite the disturbances, the match kicked off as scheduled, with Marseille securing a 1-0 victory over the Bulgarian side.
The violence drew condemnation from French President Emmanuel Macron and his Bulgarian counterpart, Iliana Iotova . Levski Sofia coach Julio Velázquez also condemned the incidents, describing the scenes as “unacceptable for football” . The disturbances overshadowed the European fixture and renewed concerns over spectator safety at international club matches.

Erling Haaland blasted beleaguered City’s form, but ahead of Arsenal test, manager Enzo Maresca says striker is happy.
Enzo Maresca insisted on Friday that Erling Haaland is “happy” at Manchester City after the striker expressed frustration over his side’s recent struggles.
Haaland gave a candid assessment of City’s malaise following Tuesday’s 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League, which came on the back of a Premier League draw at home with Fulham.
After winning 10 of their first 11 matches in all competitions this season, Maresca’s men have won just two of their last seven.
With a crucial trip to Premier League leaders Arsenal looming on Sunday, Haaland’s criticism added to the growing sense that City’s season is in danger of spiralling out of control.
“We have to do better and find some ways to control the game more and perform in a better way,” Haaland said.
“I have no idea what we were missing but you could feel it in the last few games that something was not clicking fully.”
Haaland has scored just once in his last five games for City and is without a league goal in his past three matches.
The Norway star’s body language has been noticeably angst-ridden in recent weeks, prompting suggestions that he is growing disillusioned with life at the Etihad Stadium.
City are also awaiting the result of their appeal against a guilty verdict over breaches of Premier League financial rules, with the punishment potentially including a huge points deduction.
Despite City’s woes, Maresca is adamant Haaland remains committed to the cause regardless of speculation that he could seek a move at the end of the season.
“Erling is a nine; they live for goals and winning games. If they don’t score, they are upset. I think he gesticulates in the same way when we are winning games,” Maresca told reporters on Friday.
“For sure he is not happy because we are not winning games. But it is not just Erling. Everyone is on the same page.
“He has been good. He has been normal since day one. Two or three weeks ago, he was dancing inside the pitch and in the training sessions.
“He is happy. It is normal that results affect the mood a little bit but I don’t see any problem with Erling. He is a winner.”
Maresca will need Haaland back to his best against Arsenal if third-placed City are to earn a vital victory over the champions.
Already trailing six points behind Arsenal, a defeat in north London would be a huge blow to their title hopes.
Maresca has come under fire during City’s slump in his first season after replacing Pep Guardiola.
The former Chelsea boss claimed teething problems were inevitable during the transition from Guardiola’s dynastic reign.
“Transition requires time. It’s probably because we won seven games in a row, everyone was thinking at City there’s no transition,” Maresca said.
“But I’ve said many times I’m not a magician. There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new.
“For sure, when you don’t win games, it’s not the ideal situation. For me, it’s completely normal, I’m completely relaxed, no panic at all.”

Arsenal and Man City face off in the Premier League this weekend with the Gunners holding a six-point lead over Enzo Maresca's side; Mikel Arteta says the game is important for the title fight; watch Arsenal vs Man City live on Sky Sports this Sunday, kick-off 4.30pm
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Enzo Maresca said Premier League title rivals Manchester City and Arsenal couldn’t be compared after his side's early-season form raised expectations.
Maresca described Sunday's fixture, live on Sky Sports , as "four months vs seven years", referencing the transition City are going through following Pep Guardiola's departure and the longevity of head coach Mikel Arteta at Arsenal.
"We have been top of the league for two and a half months until November 1. Now we are not there and everyone is comparing," said Maresca.
"For me, it's seven years together against four months together so you cannot compare. I understand everyone is trying to do that, but from my point of view everything is clear."
City have fallen six points behind Arsenal after failing to win in their last four league games while they've only won two of their last seven in all competitions.
"It's more than easy to understand why because we've had four months together," said Maresca when addressing his side's form.
"Transition requires time. Probably because we won seven games in a row, eight with the Champions League, everyone was thinking that there was no transition.
"I said many times, I'm not a magician. There's a transition, it's normal. We have eight or nine new players, the manager is new, so you need time.
"You can see with different clubs when they transition, how complicated it is. For me, it's completely normal.
"I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all, understanding that we need to win games because it's our business. For me, it's all normal."
In midweek, Erling Haaland made some concerning comments, claiming that "you have to question everything" after their draw against Napoli in the Champions League. But Maresca insists there is no issue with the striker.
"It's normal that results affect the mood, that's why we need to win games," said Maresca. "I don't see any problem with Erling."
"Erling is a winner. It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games. Not just Erling, everyone. Don't forget, three weeks ago, he was dancing on the pitch."
Maresca is prioritising the long-term vision he has for City. "The present is important but the future is much more important in terms of improving and building something with the team.
"Where we can be on Sunday night if we win, lose or draw, it's important but it's a long season. We'll see where we are in February and March and from there you can set the goals.
"Now, I think it's useless speaking about targets or where we can be at the end of the season."
But facing champions Arsenal on Sunday will give them idea of their progress.
"You need to show personality," he said. "That's why it's also a nice game for us to see where we are in terms of personality and from there try to understand the situation."
In the red corner, Arsenal manager Arteta knows how important matches are against their rivals in their bid to retain the Premier League title for the first time.
"When we played the home games against big teams, that becomes crucial in the title challenge," he said. "We know how important the home games are to make the difference.
"But we're in November, we know how long we have to play. But that's for every single team."
Asked whether City's form has anything to do with the club being found guilty of 115 serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules in September, Arteta admitted that "it's a question for City."
He then went on to say: "All I can say is when I watch them play is a lot of games that they have done more merits than the opponent, but this is football. To win games, that's merit to the way they play."
Asked if City are Arsenal's closest challengers for the title, Arteta replied: "We don't know, I think the challenge is for us, and the opportunity is for us.
"We cannot control what the opponents are going to do; we just need to give ourselves the best version, and I'm sure the atmosphere is going to be incredible on Sunday, and we need to enjoy and embrace those kinds of games and go for it."
Arteta did not, however, want to be drawn on the atmosphere the Emirates Stadium could produce in the wake of City's guilty verdict. The club deny all the charges and have lodged an appeal against the verdict. No sanctions have yet been announced.
On the pitch, Arsenal are sweating on the fitness of goalkeeper David Raya while centre-back William Saliba will have to wait patiently to work his way back into the side following injury.
For City, the game comes too soon for winger Antoine Semenyo, who could return next week.

Europe wants to become more independent, competitive and secure. Yet it is precisely the tasks that are crucial to this that face the deepest cuts in the draft for the next EU budget. Behind this lies a structural problem in European politics.
The special Brussels summit on the European budget for the years 2028 to 2034 ended without agreement. On 17 December, the heads of state and government will meet again. Until then, the main question will be how much Europe is prepared to spend.
The European Commission has proposed a financial framework of just under €2 trillion. Council President António Costa has reduced this to around €1.78 trillion. Germany and other net contributors still consider that too high.
More revealing than the overall figure, however, is where Costa makes the cuts. Compared with the Commission’s draft, he removes around €95.5 billion from competitiveness, prosperity and security, and around €54 billion from agriculture, cohesion and related tasks. That amounts to reductions of 16 and 5% respectively. In defence industry, security and space, the cuts are almost 30%.
Costa’s draft does foresee substantial increases for defence and competitiveness compared with the current budget. Even so, the new strategic priorities are being cut disproportionately.
Germany and other net contributors want to limit their payments and focus the budget more strongly on competitiveness and security. Poland and other cohesion countries defend the funding for their regions. France wants an ambitious European budget while also protecting its agriculture. Italy takes a sceptical view of additional European levies.
Each of these positions is understandable from a national perspective. The problem arises from how they interact.
The European financial framework requires unanimity in the Council and the consent of the European Parliament. Every government can make its approval conditional on its own interests being safeguarded. This favours spending whose benefits can be clearly attributed to individual member states.
A French president can explain to farmers which subsidies he has secured in Brussels. A Polish prime minister can point to new roads and modernised regions. But which head of government can claim the benefit of a joint European air defence system purely for his or her own country?
Joint European tasks do have political advocates. But their benefits are less easily mapped onto the national balance sheet that underpins almost every budget negotiation in the end: how much did we pay in, and how much do we get back?
About 60% of the current European financial framework is devoted to agriculture and cohesion. Both areas serve core purposes of European integration: food security, economic development and the reduction of regional disparities.
However, Europe now has additional tasks to tackle that did not carry anything like the same weight when this budget structure was created.
Russia is threatening Europe’s security order. China has built up significant technological and industrial capacity in strategic sectors. The United States is pursuing its own economic and security interests, which do not necessarily coincide with Europes.
The conditions under which the bloc has built its prosperity in recent decades are changing fundamentally.
That cannot be addressed simply through higher national defence spending. It is equally about joint defence research, industrial production capacity, secure supply chains, cross-border energy networks, military mobility and European expertise in key technologies.
In 2024 Mario Draghi set out what would be needed: catching up the innovation gap with the United States and China, combining decarbonisation with competitiveness, and strengthening Europe’s security by reducing strategic dependencies. He put the additional private and public investment required at €750 to 800 billion a year.
This sum cannot and should not be financed solely from the European budget. However, the budget can mobilise national and private investment and make joint projects possible where individual member states cannot achieve the necessary scale on their own.
I believe the European budget should be shaped much more by its tasks. The decisive factor should be what the member states can achieve better, more efficiently or more cheaply together than alone.
Agriculture and the less developed regions of Europe still need reliability. But their shares of the budget should, with appropriate transition periods, gradually yet clearly decline in order to create more scope for joint investment in the future.
Anyone who thinks Europe can simply carry on as before is living off a substance that is steadily shrinking. A Europe that wants to become more sovereign and more independent also has to get ahead of events.
That calls for honesty on the revenue side. Costa’s draft sets aside €158 billion solely for repaying the EU debt taken on during the pandemic. This money is not available for other tasks.
Costa therefore proposes additional European sources of revenue, including levies on digital services provided by large companies, on tobacco and on non-recycled electronic waste. Anyone who rejects additional own resources has to explain whether they prefer higher national contributions or corresponding cuts. And anyone who demands more European tasks has to say how they should be funded.
The contribution rebates also belong in this context. They are the expression of a budget logic that measures the success of European policy by national returns. As long as this calculation dominates, funding joint tasks will remain structurally more difficult.
Germany and France are pushing for an understanding before the end of the year. Given the French presidential election next spring, that is understandable.
One possible compromise would be an even smaller overall volume combined with concessions to the net contributors, agriculture and the cohesion countries. Particularly contentious sources of revenue could be postponed, and funding for further aid to Ukraine could be negotiated separately.
Such an agreement would carry weight. It would create planning certainty and show that 27 governments, despite differing interests, are capable of reaching a compromise.
The crucial question, however, would be the price at which it is achieved. If the main effect is to protect established spending while once again making the new strategic tasks bear most of the savings, the underlying problem would remain.
Europe would still have to tackle many of its new tasks largely through national budgets, loans and additional financing instruments. Especially for long term investment in security, infrastructure and technological competitiveness, a lack of joint planning can lead to higher costs and avoidable duplication.
We do not have to turn all our challenges into European ones. But we should organise and fund at European level those we can no longer adequately handle at national level.
Anyone who wants a more sovereign and more independent Europe must also be prepared to draw fiscal policy conclusions from that.

Senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye pledge to protect the kingdom’s security during talks in Islamabad.
Senior government and defence officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have denounced the continuing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia and renewed their pledge to support the kingdom in safeguarding its security and sovereignty.
The statement followed a meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) of the Mecca defence pact countries in the Pakistani capital, Islamabad, on Friday.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three. The committee comprises the three nations’ foreign and defence ministers alongside top military officials.
Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar thanked the participating officials after the roughly two-and-a-half-hour meeting.
“The SPDC meeting reviewed the evolving regional security situation and reaffirmed the determination of the three countries to continue working collectively towards regional peace, security and stability,” he told reporters.
“The three sides reiterated their strong condemnation of the persistent and heinous attacks by the Houthi militia, targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“They reaffirmed their collective resolve to continue and intensify efforts to support the kingdom in safeguarding its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, in accordance with the collective defence provisions of the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defence.”
The high-level talks come as Saudi Arabia continues to face attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis, who have repeatedly targeted Saudi cities, oil facilities and shipping since fighting in Yemen intensified in July.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.
These attacks were expected to top Friday’s agenda, but no details were released regarding any concrete measures.
At an emergency meeting of the pact’s members in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.
Pakistan has previously pledged to defend Saudi territory, while ruling out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also told Turkish media last week that Ankara’s current policy was aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia.
“No decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia,” he said.
Dar said Friday’s discussions also focused on implementing decisions made at previous meetings of the alliance, as well as boosting cooperation across various sectors.
“The parties reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in defence industries, joint technological development, training, and capacity building, with a view to enhancing the collective capabilities and cohesion of their armed forces in order to address mutual security concerns and contribute to peace and security in the region,” he said.

Quebec’s ban on teachers and police wearing religious symbols such as hijabs and turbans at work remains in place.
A landmark ruling by Canada’s Supreme Court has largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law, leaving in place a ban on public school teachers, police officers and some other public employees wearing religious symbols at work.
The ruling settles a years-long legal battle over a law that has forced some workers to choose between their careers and how they practise their faith.
The court left the ban in place, but upheld an exception to a separate rule requiring elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly to uncover their faces, finding the requirement infringed upon their democratic rights.
The National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), one of the groups that challenged Bill 21, called the ruling “a dark day in our constitutional democracy”.
Speaking after the ruling, NCCM’s chief executive Stephen Brown said, “ In our country, in the 21st century, entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are.”
The court also weighed in on a question that goes beyond Quebec — how far governments can go in using the notwithstanding clause.
The clause is part of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It lets federal and provincial governments keep a law in force even if it violates certain Charter rights, including freedom of religion and the right to equality, shielding it from court challenges. The override lasts up to five years and can be renewed. Quebec used it when it passed Bill 21 in 2019 and renewed it in 2024.
On Friday, the Supreme Court found Quebec had used the clause lawfully and that it can be used before a court rules on whether a law violates Charter rights.
“It is not open to the courts to place additional limits on the exercise of the override power,” said the decision.
Four of the seven justices also agreed that judges can formally declare that a law violates those rights even if the clause keeps the law in effect. Such a declaration would leave the law in place, but “vindicate affected individuals” and let citizens know how their rights are being temporarily overridden by their representatives, the justices wrote.
Only three of the justices would have issued one in this case, so the court issued none.
The Canadian Civil Liberties Association, which also challenged Bill 21, said the ruling “sends a message that even shielded laws cannot escape scrutiny entirely”.
“But for the people this law affects every day, that door remains closed,” said the CCLA. “Bill 21 has already denied a generation of Quebecers their chosen profession in public service because of their faith. That is discrimination, and it is why we took on this case.”
Quebec passed Bill 21 in June 2019 , saying it would protect the religious neutrality of public institutions. It bars people in certain public jobs from wearing religious symbols such as hijabs, turbans and kippahs while at work. Teachers who were already in their posts on March 27, 2019, were able to continue wearing them as long as they stayed in the same role with the same employer.
The law has reshaped lives , leading to people losing their jobs and in some cases, leaving Quebec to continue working in their professions. Some Muslim women have decided to take off their hijabs while at work in order to keep their jobs.
Quebec has since widened the restrictions to support staff and volunteers at school under Bill 94 and to daycare staff under Bill 9. In both cases, Quebec invoked the notwithstanding clause.
Quebec’s government has said it wants to go further by barring elementary school students from wearing religious symbols.
Nevien Waly, who wears a hijab and was told she could not volunteer at her children’s school under Bill 94, said she had expected the court to uphold the law, but was holding out hope that it might go the other way.
“I didn’t think that it would be overturned, but I’m still disappointed,” she told Al Jazeera after the ruling. “I’m sad for myself, worried about the future of our kids.”
Waly said she worried the ruling would embolden people to openly mistreat those who wear religious symbols, something she said she had already experienced more often in recent years, as she started wearing the hijab and Quebec widened its restrictions.
The case was heard by seven justices. Chief Justice Richard Wagner, writing for three justices, said Bill 21 was rooted in Quebec’s “legitimate and historical commitment” to keeping the state secular. He concluded that the Quebec government had “validly used” its power to keep the law in force.
In a partial dissent, Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin wrote there was no serious question that the law violates the right to freedom of religion. They described how Muslim women had been turned away from jobs because they wear a hijab and how the law had prevented people from taking promotions or being transferred to new roles because they would lose their exemptions. They said the law “non-trivially influences life choices and mobility”.
“The Act’s effects are not experienced equally,” they wrote. “They fall most heavily on Muslim women.”
The justices acknowledged that the consequences went beyond work, noting reports of more verbal and physical abuse from some members of religious minorities. They said the law affected people’s “basic sense of belonging in Canadian and Quebec society”.
Before the ruling, Waly said she could not imagine leaving Quebec, where she grew up and where much of her family lives. On Friday, she said she was encouraging her children to excel in school so they would have the option to leave.

The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.
Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.
The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.
Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.
Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.
But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.
"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.
Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.
"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.
The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."
Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran .
Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.
In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.
It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.
This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.
